verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} one{H259} voice{H6963} from the house{H1004} of prayer{H8605}, and it said{H559} to the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397}: Go{H1980} and pour out{H3332} from the bowls{H7086} upon the ground{H127} the burning-anger{H2740} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה (beit ha-tefillah — 'house of prayer', H8605). Greek has ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ ('from the temple'). This is the Isaiah 56:7 phrase — 'my house shall be called a house of prayer (בֵּית תְּפִלָּה) for all peoples' — which Yeshua quotes in Matt 21:13. A back-translator from Greek ναός would write הֵיכָל (heikal — 'temple') or מִקְדָּשׁ (mikdash — 'sanctuary'), not the Isaiah-specific 'house of prayer.' Same distinction appears in Rev 21:22.

Uses חֲרוֹן יַהְוֶה (charon YHWH — 'the burning-anger of YHWH', H2740). Greek has τοῦ θυμοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ('the wrath of God'). The Hebrew חרון is the specific 'burning/fierce anger' of YHWH in the Torah (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26). A back-translator from Greek θυμός would use חֵמָה (chemah — 'wrath/fury'), not the distinctly OT compound חרון.

Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground', H127), not אֶרֶץ (erets). Greek has γῆν (ge — 'earth'). Same word choice seen in Rev 21:1. The author consistently uses the Genesis creation-soil word where Greek has the generic term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the house of prayer' (מבית התפלה). Greek: 'from the temple' (ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ). Different building designation.
Greek adds μεγάλης ('great/loud') to describe the voice — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' preserves the Isaiah 56:7 echo. This same term (beit ha-tefillah) reappears in Rev 21:22.
צָאקוּ appears to be a variant imperative form related to יצק (yatsaq, H3332 — to pour). The aleph insertion is characteristic of later Hebrew phonological development.
textual_notes: The seven bowls of burning-anger parallel the seven plagues of Egypt. The Hebrew author frames the entire sequence using Exodus plague vocabulary, beginning with the Torah's specific anger-term חרון.

verses.translation: And the first{H7223} went{H1980} and poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} upon the ground{H127}, and it became{H1961} boils{H7822} breaking-out{H6524} upon the man{H120} who had upon them the mark from the beast{H2416}, and those praying{H6419} to his graven-image{H6459}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שְׁחִין פֹּרֵחַ (shechin poreach — 'boils breaking out'). This is the EXACT phrase from Exodus 9:9-10, the sixth plague of Egypt: שְׁחִין פֹּרֵחַ אֲבַעְבֻּעֹת ('boils breaking out in sores'). Greek has ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρόν ('a bad and evil sore'). A back-translator from the generic Greek 'sore' would NEVER reconstruct the specific Exodus plague phrase. The Hebrew author deliberately frames the first bowl as a repetition of the sixth Egyptian plague.

Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'graven image', H6459) — the specific word from the second commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל ('you shall not make for yourself a graven image', Ex 20:4, Deut 5:8). Greek has εἰκόνα ('image' — generic). A back-translator from Greek would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image'), not the Decalogue-specific pesel.

Uses הַמִּתְפַּלְּלִים (hammitpallelim — 'those praying to', hitpael of palal H6419) for idol worship. Greek has προσκυνοῦντας ('those bowing/worshipping'). The Hebrew uses the PRAYER verb — the same root as תְּפִילָּה (tefillah — prayer) in verse 1. The author creates a deliberate contrast: true prayer (tefillah) belongs in the house of prayer to YHWH; false prayer (hitpallel) goes to the graven image.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שחין פרח ('boils breaking out' — Exodus plague language). Greek: ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρόν ('a bad and evil sore'). The Hebrew carries the Exodus plague echo; the Greek is generic.
Hebrew: פסל ('graven image' — Decalogue term). Greek: εἰκόνα ('image' — generic term).
translation_notes: 'Boils breaking out' preserves the exact Exodus 9:9-10 phrase.
סִּימָן (siman — 'mark/sign') is a post-biblical Hebrew word. No standard Strong's number. Greek χάραγμα means 'stamp/brand' — a different concept than a sign or marker.
'Graven image' for pesel — the Decalogue word, not a generic 'image.'
textual_notes: Exodus 9:9-10: 'And it shall become fine dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall become boils breaking out (שְׁחִין פֹּרֵחַ) in sores on man and on beast.' The first bowl plague directly replicates the sixth Egyptian plague.

verses.translation: And the second{H8145} messenger{H4397} poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} in the sea{H3220}, and it became{H1961} blood{H1818} like from a dead one{H4191}, and all{H3605} that{H834} was in the sea{H3220} died{H4191}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר בַּיָּם תָּמוּת ('and all that was in the sea died'). Greek: πᾶσα ψυχὴ ζῶσα ἀπέθανεν ('every living soul died'). Hebrew uses the general 'all that was' (כל אשר); Greek specifies 'every living soul' (ψυχὴ ζῶσα). The Hebrew echoes the flood narrative style where 'all' perishes without the Greek's added precision.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all that was in the sea died.' Greek: 'every living soul died, the things in the sea.' Greek adds ψυχὴ ζῶσα ('living soul') absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: The sea turning to blood echoes the first Egyptian plague (Ex 7:20-21) where the Nile became blood and all fish died. The Hebrew author extends the Nile plague to the entire sea.

verses.translation: And the third{H7992} poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} in the wells{H875} of water{H4325}, and it became{H1961} blood{H1818}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּאֵרוֹת מַיִם (be'erot mayim — 'wells of water', H875). Greek has ποταμούς καὶ πηγὰς τῶν ὑδάτων ('rivers and springs of waters'). The Hebrew has only 'wells' — the specific word for dug wells (Gen 21:30, 26:15-22, Num 21:16-18). A back-translator from Greek, which lists both 'rivers and springs,' would use נהרות ומעינות ('rivers and springs'), NOT the single Hebrew word be'erot. The well (be'er) is a distinctly Patriarchal term — Isaac digs wells, Moses finds his wife at a well. The Hebrew reduction to wells alone points to authorial choice, not translation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'wells of water' (בארות מים — one term). Greek: 'rivers and springs of waters' (ποταμούς καὶ πηγάς — two terms). Hebrew is more concise and uses a different category.
translation_notes: 'Wells' for be'erot preserves the Patriarchal and Exodus resonance — water sources in the wilderness.
textual_notes: Exodus 7:19: 'Stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt — over their rivers, their canals, their pools, and all their reservoirs of water.' The first Egyptian plague struck all water sources. The Hebrew uses wells (be'erot) — perhaps the most vital water source in the land.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} that the messenger{H4397} says{H559}: YHWH{H3068} the righteous{H6662}, the Was{H1961} and the Is{H1933}, and holy{H6918} are you{H859}, that you gave{H5414} this judgment{H4941}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The formula הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה ('the Was and the Is') uses the root ה-ו-ה (havah, H1933) — the very root behind the divine name YHWH. The participial form הוה shares the consonants of the Tetragrammaton. A Hebrew reader immediately sees the wordplay: YHWH is named because He IS (hoveh) and WAS (hayah). Greek ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν ('the being and the was') cannot replicate this connection to the divine name. A back-translator from Greek would use הַהֹוֶה וְהַהָיָה (reversing the order to match Greek) and would NEVER recreate this pun on the name YHWH.
Hebrew: 'the messenger' (המלאך) — no qualifier. Greek: 'the angel of the waters' (τοῦ ἀγγέλου τῶν ὑδάτων). Greek adds 'of the waters' which is entirely absent from the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the messenger' (no qualifier). Greek: 'the angel of the waters.' Significant addition in Greek.
Hebrew order: 'Was and Is' (past then present). Greek order: 'being and was' (present then past). Different sequence.
Hebrew: 'holy' (קדוש). Greek: ὅσιος ('holy/devout') — but also Greek TR commonly has 'ὁ ἐσόμενος' ('the one to come') in the fuller formula, here shortened.
translation_notes: 'The Was and the Is' preserves the Hebrew's deliberate use of being-verbs that echo the divine name YHWH (from root הוה — 'to be').

The Hebrew lacks 'and who is to come' which sometimes appears in the Greek formula (Rev 1:4,8, 4:8). Its absence here may be deliberate — judgment is already underway, so the coming is no longer future.
textual_notes: Exodus 3:14: אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה ('I will be what I will be'). The name YHWH itself derives from the root היה/הוה. The Hebrew author's formula plays directly on this etymology.

verses.translation: For they poured-out{H8210} the blood{H1818} of the holy-ones{H6918} and the prophets{H5030} like water{H4325}, and you gave{H5414} them blood{H1818} to drink{H8354}, for they are deserving of this.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT OT QUOTATION: שָׁפְכוּ דְּמֵי... כַּמַּיִם ('they poured out blood... like water') is from Psalm 79:3: שָׁפְכוּ דָמָם כַּמַּיִם סְבִיבוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָם ('they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem'). The Hebrew preserves this Psalm quotation with the root שפך (shafach, H8210) plus the simile כמים ('like water'). Greek simply has αἷμα... ἐξέχεαν ('they poured out blood') WITHOUT the 'like water' simile. A back-translator from the Greek, which lacks this simile, could never produce the Psalm 79 quotation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'poured out the blood... like water' (כמים — Psalm 79:3 quotation). Greek: 'poured out the blood' — no 'like water' simile.
Greek: ἄξιοί εἰσι ('they are worthy'). Hebrew: ראויים ('deserving'). Similar meaning but different words — ראויים is a post-biblical Hebrew term.
translation_notes: רְאוּיִם (re'uyim — 'deserving/worthy') is a post-biblical Hebrew adjective. No standard Strong's number.
'Poured out' for shafach (H8210) — the blood-spilling verb, used for murder (Gen 9:6, 37:22) and sacrifice.
textual_notes: Psalm 79:3 — 'They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.' The Hebrew author applies this psalm of national lamentation to the end-time judgment — the nations who shed blood like water now drink blood.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} another{H312} messenger{H4397} who spoke{H1696} from within{H8432} the palace{H1964}: Yes{H3651}, Elohim{H430} of Hosts{H6635}, your judgments{H4941} are righteousness{H6664}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַהֵיכָל (ha-heikal — 'the palace/temple', H1964) — the word for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:3,5,17) and for royal palaces. Greek has θυσιαστηρίου ('the altar'). Major divergence — Hebrew says the voice comes from the temple/palace; Greek says from the altar. A back-translator from Greek would write מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach — 'altar'), not heikal.

Uses אֱלֹהֵי הַצְּבָאוֹת (Elohei ha-Tsevaot — 'Elohim of Hosts', H6635) — the compound divine name appearing throughout the prophets (Isa 1:9, Jer 5:14, Amos 3:13). Greek has Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי or אֵל שַׁדַּי, NOT the specific prophetic name 'Elohim of Hosts.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from within the palace' (מתוך ההיכל). Greek: 'from the altar' (ἐκ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου). Different source location.
Greek adds ἀληθιναί ('true') to 'true and righteous are your judgments.' Hebrew has only 'your judgments are righteousness' — no 'true.'
translation_notes: 'Palace' for heikal reflects the dual meaning of the Hebrew word — both temple and royal palace. The heavenly heikal is both God's dwelling and his throne room.
textual_notes: Psalm 19:10 (ET 19:9): מִשְׁפְּטֵי יְהוָה אֱמֶת צָדְקוּ יַחְדָּו — 'The judgments of YHWH are truth, they are righteous altogether.' The messenger's declaration echoes this psalm.

verses.translation: And the fourth{H7243} poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} upon the sun{H8121}, and to it was given{H5414} to make{H6213} heat upon the man{H120}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לעשות חם ('to make heat') — the Hebrew verb עשה (asah, H6213 — 'to do/make') with חם (chom — 'heat'). Greek has καυματίσαι ('to scorch/burn'). The Hebrew is indirect — the sun was given permission 'to make heat'; the Greek is violent — 'to scorch men.' The Hebrew framing treats the sun as an instrument given divine permission, consistent with the OT pattern of natural forces acting under God's command (Ps 148:8).

Uses הָאָדָם (ha-adam — 'the man', H120) with the definite article, as in verse 2. Greek has τοὺς ἀνθρώπους (plural 'men'). The Hebrew consistently uses the collective singular ha-adam echoing the Genesis creation account.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐν πυρί ('with fire') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew has only 'heat,' not 'fire.'

verses.translation: And there was{H1961} much{H7235} heat upon the man{H120}, and they cursed{H7043} YHWH{H3068} on account of these plagues{H5061}, and did not do{H6213} repentance{H8666} to give{H5414} him glory{H3519}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', H8666, from root שוב H7725). Greek has μετενόησαν (metanoeo — 'changed mind'). These are fundamentally different concepts: Hebrew repentance is about RETURNING to God (שוב — the quintessential prophetic call, Hos 14:2, Joel 2:12-13, Mal 3:7); Greek repentance is about CHANGING ONE'S MIND. A back-translator from Greek would use a mind/thought verb, not the return-to-God concept teshuvah.

Uses מְקַלְּלוּ (meqallelu — 'they cursed', H7043) — the OT curse verb (Gen 12:3, Lev 24:11,14). Greek has ἐβλασφήμησαν ('they blasphemed'). Hebrew 'curse' and Greek 'blaspheme' carry different weight — cursing God invokes the Levitical death penalty (Lev 24:15-16); blasphemy is a concept shaped more by Greek thought.

Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues', H5061) — the Levitical term for the Exodus plagues (Ex 11:1) and skin afflictions requiring priestly inspection (Lev 13-14). Greek has πληγάς (plegas — 'blows/strokes'). A back-translator from Greek would more likely use מַכּוֹת (makot — 'blows'), not the Levitical nega'im.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they cursed YHWH' (direct, using curse verb + divine name). Greek: 'they blasphemed the NAME of God who has authority over these plagues' (expanded, using blasphemy verb + God's name + relative clause). Hebrew is more concise; Greek adds 'the name' and an entire relative clause absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'repentance' (תשובה — return). Greek: μετενόησαν ('changed mind'). Different concept.
translation_notes: 'Repentance' for teshuvah captures the Hebrew concept of returning to God, not merely changing one's mind.
'Plagues' for nega'im preserves the Exodus/Levitical connection.
textual_notes: Joel 2:12-13: 'Return to me (שובו אלי) with all your heart... rend your heart and not your garments, and return (שובו) to YHWH your Elohim.' The Hebrew concept of repentance as teshuvah (return) is central to the prophetic tradition.

verses.translation: And the fifth{H2549} poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} upon the throne{H3678} of the beast{H2416}, and it darkened{H2821} it, and they were biting{H5391} their tongues{H3956} because of distress.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נוֹשְׁכִים (noshchim — 'biting', from nashach H5391) — the specific verb for a SERPENT's bite (Gen 49:17, Num 21:6-9, Ecc 10:8,11, Amos 5:19). Greek has ἐμασῶντο ('gnawed/chewed'). The Hebrew serpent-bite verb creates an ironic image: the followers of the beast (serpent/dragon) are now themselves bitten. A back-translator from the Greek 'gnaw/chew' would use לעס (la'as — 'chew') or כסס, not the serpent-specific nashach.

Darkness plague: The fifth bowl brings darkness (חשך, H2821), echoing the ninth Egyptian plague (Ex 10:21-23): וַיְהִי חֹשֶׁךְ אֲפֵלָה ('and there was thick darkness'). The Hebrew author sequences the bowl plagues to mirror Exodus.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'and it darkened it' (והחשך אותו — the throne/realm is darkened). Greek: 'and his kingdom became darkened' (ἡ βασιλεία αὐτοῦ ἐσκοτωμένη). Greek specifies 'his kingdom'; Hebrew darkens 'it' (the throne area).
Hebrew: 'because of distress' (צער). Greek: 'because of the distress' and adds 'because of their sores' (ἐκ τῶν ἑλκῶν αὐτῶν). Greek references the sores from the first bowl; Hebrew does not.
translation_notes: צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/pain') is a post-biblical Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.

Greek 16:11 — 'And they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and sores, and did not repent of their works' — is ENTIRELY ABSENT from the Hebrew text. The Hebrew moves directly from the fifth bowl (v10) to the sixth bowl (v11). This missing verse is significant.
textual_notes: Exodus 10:21-23: The ninth plague of darkness. The Hebrew author places the darkness bowl fifth (not ninth) but uses the same root חשך, maintaining the Exodus plague vocabulary.

The absence of Greek 16:11 from the Hebrew text is noteworthy. The Hebrew has 20 verses for this chapter; the Greek has 21. Greek 16:11 repeats the blasphemy-and-no-repentance formula already present in Hebrew v9 — the Hebrew author may have seen this as redundant.

verses.translation: And the sixth{H8345} poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} upon the river{H5104} Euphrates{H6578}, and it dried up{H3001} the river{H5104}, in order to be a highway{H4546} for the kings{H4428} who are from the rising{H4217} of the sun{H8121}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מְסִלָּה (mesillah — 'highway/raised road', H4546). Greek has ὁδός ('way/road'). The mesillah is the specific Isaiah highway: Isaiah 11:16 — 'And there shall be a highway (מסלה) for the remnant of his people from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.' Isaiah 62:10 — 'Build up, build up the highway (מסלה)!' A back-translator from Greek ὁδός would use דֶּרֶךְ (derekh — 'way/road'), not the Isaianic mesillah. The drying of the Euphrates with a mesillah for eastern kings directly echoes the Exodus crossing and Isaiah's prophesied highway.

Uses ויבש (vayyubash — 'and it dried up', from yavesh H3001). This is the Exodus verb — Joshua 2:10: 'YHWH dried up (הוֹבִישׁ) the waters of the Red Sea before you.' Joshua 4:23: 'YHWH your God dried up (הוֹבִישׁ) the Jordan.' The Euphrates drying is framed as a new Exodus crossing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a highway' (מסלה — Isaiah's specific term). Greek: ἑτοιμασθῇ ἡ ὁδός ('the way might be prepared'). Greek adds 'prepared' and uses a generic word for 'way.'
Greek: 'the great river Euphrates' (τὸν ποταμὸν τὸν μέγαν). Hebrew: 'the river Euphrates' (הנהר פרת) — lacking 'great.'
Hebrew: 'it dried up the river' (ויבש את הנהר). Greek: 'its water was dried up' (ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτοῦ). Hebrew dries the river itself; Greek dries its water.
translation_notes: 'Highway' for mesillah preserves the Isaiah highway prophecy connection.
'From the rising of the sun' (ממזרח השמש) is the Hebrew idiom for 'from the east' — more vivid than the simple directional word.
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:15-16: 'And YHWH will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River (Euphrates) with his scorching wind, and will strike it into seven channels... And there shall be a highway (מסלה) for the remnant of his people.' The drying of the Euphrates for a highway is directly from Isaiah.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} that there went{H1980} from the mouth{H6310} of the serpent{H8577}, and from the mouth{H6310} of the beast{H2416}, and from the mouth{H6310} of the false{H8267} prophet{H5030}, three{H7969} unclean{H2931} creeping-things{H8318} in the likeness{H1823} of frogs{H6854}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שְׁרָצִים (sheratzim — 'creeping/swarming things', H8318). Greek has πνεύματα τρία ἀκάθαρτα ('three unclean SPIRITS'). The Hebrew sheretz is the Torah's specific classification for unclean swarming creatures — Genesis 1:20-21 (creation), Leviticus 11:29-43 (dietary laws). A back-translator from Greek 'spirits' (πνεύματα) would write רוּחוֹת (ruchot — 'spirits'), NEVER the Levitical classification sheratzim. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire chapter: the Hebrew author categorizes these entities using Torah taxonomy, not Greek pneumatology.

Uses תַּנִּין (tannin — 'serpent/sea-creature', H8577) — the primordial creature from Genesis 1:21 (great sea creatures), Isaiah 27:1 (Leviathan the tannin), Isaiah 51:9 (Rahab the tannin), Ezekiel 29:3, 32:2 (Pharaoh as tannin). Greek uses δράκων ('dragon'). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as דרקון, not reach for the OT's primordial creature word tannin.

Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut — 'in the likeness of', H1823) — from the root דמות used in Genesis 1:26 (בִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — 'in our likeness'). This is the creation-theology 'likeness' word. Greek has simple ὡς ('as/like'). A back-translator would write כְּמוֹ (kemo — 'like'), not the theologically loaded kidmut.

Uses צְפַרְדְּעִים (tsefarde'im — 'frogs', H6854) — a word appearing in the OT only in the Exodus plague narrative (Ex 7:27-8:10, Ps 78:45, 105:30). This is exclusively Exodus vocabulary. The frog imagery combined with sheratzim creates a double Exodus plague reference.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: שרצים ('creeping things' — Torah creature classification). Greek: πνεύματα ('spirits'). Entirely different ontological category.
Hebrew: תנין ('serpent/sea-creature'). Greek: δράκων ('dragon'). Different mythological framework.
contradictions: The Hebrew and Greek present fundamentally different entities: the Hebrew has unclean swarming creatures (physical, Torah-classified beings) that RESEMBLE frogs; the Greek has unclean spirits that are LIKE frogs. The Hebrew operates in Levitical purity categories; the Greek in spiritual/pneumatic categories.
translation_notes: 'Creeping things' for sheratzim — the Levitical classification term, not 'spirits.'
'Serpent' for tannin — the primordial sea creature of Hebrew cosmology.
'In the likeness of' for kidmut — the Genesis creation-likeness word.

נביא שקר ('prophet of falsehood') is the standard Hebrew construction for a false prophet (Jer 14:14, 23:25-26, 27:10,14-16). Greek ψευδοπροφήτης is a compound word; Hebrew uses the two-word construct.
textual_notes: Exodus 7:27-8:10 (ET 8:1-14): The second Egyptian plague — frogs (צפרדעים) swarming over the land. The Hebrew author frames these demonic entities using Exodus plague vocabulary: they are creeping-things (sheratzim) in the likeness of frogs (tsefarde'im).

verses.translation: And these are spirits{H7307} of the Adversary{H7854}, and they do{H6213} wonders and signs{H226}, and they go{H1980} to the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} and to all{H3605} the world{H5769}, to gather{H6908} them to the battle{H4421} on the day{H3117} of YHWH{H3068} the Mighty{H117}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַיּוֹם יַהְוֶה הָאַדִּיר ('the day of YHWH the Mighty'). Greek has τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης τῆς μεγάλης τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ Παντοκράτορος ('that great day of God the Almighty'). The Hebrew uses the OT prophetic formula 'Day of YHWH' (יום יהוה — Joel 1:15, 2:1,11,31; Amos 5:18,20; Isa 13:6,9; Zeph 1:7,14; Mal 3:23) plus the title אַדִּיר (addir — 'mighty/majestic', H117 — Ps 8:2,10, 93:4, Isa 33:21). A back-translator from Greek would write 'the great day of God Almighty' — using גָּדוֹל (gadol — great) not אַדִּיר, and אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי not יהוה.

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-Satan — 'THE Adversary', H7854) with the definite article — the specific figure from Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1-2, where the Satan is a prosecutorial figure in the divine court. Greek has δαιμονίων ('of demons'). Radically different: Hebrew attributes to the singular Adversary; Greek attributes to generic demons.

Uses אוֹתוֹת (otot — 'signs', H226) — the word for the signs of the Exodus (Ex 4:8-9,17,28,30, 7:3, 10:1-2). Greek has σημεῖα ('signs'). While similar in meaning, the Hebrew word carries the specific Exodus-signs resonance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirits of the Adversary' (רוחות השטן). Greek: 'spirits of demons' (πνεύματα δαιμονίων). Different attribution.
Hebrew: 'the day of YHWH the Mighty.' Greek: 'that great day of God the Almighty.' Different divine title and different adjective.
Hebrew: 'wonders and signs' (ניסים ואותות — two terms). Greek: 'signs' (σημεῖα — one term). Hebrew has an additional category.
translation_notes: נִיסִּים (nissim — 'wonders/miracles') is a post-biblical Hebrew noun. No standard Strong's number.
'The Mighty' for addir preserves the specific Hebrew title — used of YHWH in Psalm 93:4 and Isaiah 33:21.
textual_notes: Joel 2:11,31 (ET 3:4): 'The great and terrible day of YHWH (יוֹם יְהוָה הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא).' The Hebrew author uses the established prophetic formula but substitutes אדיר for the more common גדול ונורא.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! I will come{H935} like a thief{H1590}. And holy{H6918} are those who do not sleep{H3462}, and guard{H8104} himself so that he not go{H1980} naked{H6174} without{H1097} garments{H4403}, in order that his nakedness{H6172} not be exposed{H1540}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֶרְוָה (ervah — 'nakedness/shame', H6172) — the specific Levitical word for sexual nakedness, used 24 times in Leviticus 18 alone ('you shall not uncover the nakedness (ערות) of...'). Greek has ἀσχημοσύνη ('indecency/shame'). A back-translator from Greek would use בּוּשָׁה (bushah — 'shame') or חֶרְפָּה (cherpah — 'reproach'), not the highly specific Levitical ervah.

Uses קָדוֹשׁ (kadosh — 'holy/set-apart', H6918). Greek has μακάριος ('blessed/happy/fortunate'). Fundamentally different: Hebrew says these watchful ones are HOLY (consecrated, set apart for God); Greek says they are BLESSED (happy/fortunate). A back-translator from μακάριος would write אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'happy/blessed'), not kadosh.

Uses יְגֻלֶּה (yegulleh — 'be exposed/uncovered', from galah H1540). This is the verb from Leviticus 18:6ff — 'to uncover nakedness' (לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה). Greek has βλέπωσι ('they see'). The Hebrew uses the Levitical technical term for exposing nakedness; Greek merely says 'they see.' A back-translator from 'see' would write יראו (yir'u), not the Levitical galah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (קדוש). Greek: μακάριος ('blessed'). Different attribute.
Hebrew: 'those who do not sleep' (שלא ישנים — negative framing). Greek: ὁ γρηγορῶν ('the one watching/staying awake' — positive framing).
Hebrew has both 'naked' (ערום) AND 'without garments' (בלי מלבושים). Greek has only γυμνός ('naked'). Hebrew is more elaborate.
translation_notes: 'Naked' (arom, H6174) and 'nakedness' (ervah, H6172) use different roots but create a paranomasia in Hebrew. The double emphasis — naked AND without garments — underscores the shame.
'Guard himself' (ושמור את עצמו) — the verb שמר (shamar) is the Torah's watchman word (Gen 2:15 — Adam commanded to 'keep/guard' the garden).
textual_notes: The thief imagery echoes 1 Thess 5:2,4 and Matt 24:43. But the nakedness/garments imagery connects to Genesis 3:7,10,21 — Adam and Eve's nakedness after sin and God's provision of garments. The watchful believer avoids the Edenic shame.

verses.translation: And he gathered{H6908} them in one{H259} place{H4725} called{H7121} in the tongue{H3956} of Hebrew{H5680}: Har-Megidon.

one_way_hebrew: The name הַרְמְגִדֹּן is transparent in Hebrew: הַר (har — 'mountain', H2022) + מְגִדֹּן (Megidon/Megiddo). In Hebrew, this is immediately understood as 'Mountain of Megiddo.' Greek Ἁρμαγεδδών is an opaque transliteration that requires explanation. The self-evident meaning in Hebrew versus the opaque Greek form suggests Hebrew priority — the name originates in the language where it has meaning.

Megiddo (מגדו/מגדון) is the site of decisive OT battles: Judges 5:19 (Deborah's victory), 2 Kings 23:29 (Josiah's death), 2 Chronicles 35:22. The word itself may derive from the root גדד (gadad — 'to cut/gather troops').
translation_notes: The phrase בלשון עברי ('in the tongue of Hebrew') is noteworthy — a Hebrew text explaining that a word is Hebrew. This may indicate the author writes for an audience that reads Hebrew but may also know Greek, or it may be a rhetorical device emphasizing the Hebraic nature of the name.
'Har-Megidon' transliterated rather than translated ('Mountain of Megiddo') to preserve it as a proper noun.
textual_notes: Judges 5:19: 'The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo (מגדו).' Megiddo is the archetypal battlefield of Israel's history.
Zechariah 12:11: 'On that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddon (מגדון).' The spelling מגדון matches the Hebrew Revelation form.

verses.translation: And the seventh{H7637} poured{H3332} his bowl{H7086} into the air, and a voice{H6963} went{H1980} from the throne{H3678} and said{H559}: This has passed{H5674}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עָבַר (avar — 'has passed/crossed over', H5674). Greek has γέγονε ('it is done/it has become'). The Hebrew verb avar means to pass through, cross over — the same root as 'Hebrew' (עברי — 'one who crosses over') and the verb used for crossing the Jordan (Josh 3:14-17). This may carry connotations of an ordeal passing through, rather than a mere announcement of completion.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the throne' (מהכסא). Greek: 'from the temple of heaven, from the throne' (ἀπὸ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου). Greek adds 'from the temple of heaven.'
Hebrew: 'a voice' (קול). Greek: 'a great voice' (φωνὴ μεγάλη). Greek adds 'great.'
Hebrew: 'this has passed' (זאת עבר). Greek: γέγονε ('it is done'). Different verb with different nuance.
translation_notes: אֲוִיר (avir — 'air') is a later Hebrew/Aramaic word without a standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And there were{H1961} voices{H6963} and thunders{H7482} and lightnings{H1300}, and tremblings{H7461} of the earth{H776} that had never{H3808} been{H1961} from of old{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רַעֲדוֹת (ra'adot — 'tremblings', from ra'ad H7461). Greek has σεισμός ('earthquake' — specifically). Hebrew רעד is a broader term encompassing trembling of the earth AND of people (Ex 15:15 — 'trembling seized the chiefs of Moab'; Ps 2:11 — 'serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling'). A back-translator from the specific Greek σεισμός would use רַעַשׁ (ra'ash — 'earthquake'), not the more general ra'ad.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'that had never been from of old' (שלא היה מעולם — concise). Greek: 'such as had not been since men were on the earth, so great an earthquake' (oἷος οὐκ ἐγένετο ἀφ᾽ οὗ οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐγένοντο ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, τηλικοῦτος σεισμός, οὕτω μέγας — greatly expanded). Greek adds 'since men were on the earth' and 'so great.'
translation_notes: 'From of old' for me'olam (H5769) — the same word as 'eternity/age,' here meaning 'since time immemorial.'
textual_notes: Exodus 19:16,18 — Sinai theophany: 'There were thunders (קולות) and lightnings (ברקים)... and the whole mountain trembled (ויחרד) greatly.' The seventh bowl recapitulates the Sinai theophany with the same vocabulary.

verses.translation: And the great{H1419} city{H5892} was made{H6213} into three{H7969} parts{H2506}, and the cities{H5892} of the peoples{H5971} fell{H5307}. And the great{H1419} city{H5892} Babel{H894} was remembered{H2142} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068}, to give{H5414} her the cup{H3563} with the wine{H3196} of the burning-anger{H2740} of his wrath{H639}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ (charon appo — 'the burning-anger of his wrath/nose'). This is a distinctly OT compound: חרון (charon, H2740 — 'fierce/burning anger') + אף (af, H639 — 'nose/anger'). It appears as a fixed phrase throughout the OT: Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:18, Josh 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Jer 25:37-38, 30:24, 49:37. Greek has τοῦ θυμοῦ τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ('of the wrath of his anger'). A back-translator from the two Greek anger-words would use חֵמָה (chemah — wrath) + כַּעַס/אַף (anger), NOT the specific OT compound חרון אפו.
Uses בָּבֶל (Bavel — 'Babel', H894) — the Hebrew name that carries the Genesis 11 etymology of 'confusion' (from root בלל — to confuse). Greek Βαβυλών is a transliteration that loses this wordplay.
Uses עַמִּים (amim — 'peoples', H5971). Greek has ἐθνῶν ('nations/gentiles'). As in Rev 21, Hebrew uses the more neutral 'peoples' while Greek uses the loaded term 'nations/gentiles.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ). Hebrew preserves the divine name.
translation_notes: 'Burning-anger of his wrath' for charon appo — preserving both Hebrew anger-words. חרון is the burning quality; אף is the nose/breath of fury.
'Babel' rather than 'Babylon' to preserve the Hebrew word and its Genesis 11 connection.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:15-16: 'Take this cup of the wine of fury (כוס היין החמה) from my hand, and make all the nations drink it.' The cup of wine imagery is deeply rooted in the prophets (Isa 51:17,22; Jer 25:15-28, 49:12, 51:7; Hab 2:16).

verses.translation: And all{H3605} the mountains{H2022} and hills{H1389} fled{H5127}, and were not seen{H7200} anymore{H5750}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has הָרִים וּגְבָעוֹת ('mountains and hills'). Greek has πᾶσα νῆσος... καὶ ὄρη ('every island... and mountains'). The Hebrew pair 'mountains and hills' is an established OT merism — Isaiah 40:4 ('every mountain and hill shall be made low'), Isaiah 54:10, Ezekiel 6:3, 36:4,6, Hosea 10:8. A back-translator from the Greek 'islands and mountains' would write אִיִּים וְהָרִים ('islands and mountains'), NOT the standard prophetic pair הרים וגבעות. The Hebrew author uses the fixed prophetic formula; the Greek translator substituted 'islands' for 'hills.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'mountains and hills' (הרים וגבעות — OT merism). Greek: 'every island and mountains' (νῆσος... ὄρη). Entirely different pairing.
Hebrew: 'were not seen anymore' (ולא נראו עוד). Greek: 'were not found' (οὐχ εὑρέθησαν). Different verb — 'seen' vs. 'found.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:4: 'Every valley shall be raised up, every mountain and hill (כל הר וגבעה) shall be made low.' The mountains-and-hills pair is Isaiah's eschatological leveling imagery.
Nahum 1:5: 'The mountains quake before him and the hills (גבעות) melt.' Same prophetic pair in judgment context.

verses.translation: And great{H1419} hail{H1259} fell{H5307} upon the man{H120} from the heavens{H8064}, and they reviled{H2778} YHWH{H3068} on account of the plague{H5061} of the hail{H1259}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בָּרָד (barad — 'hail', H1259) — the seventh Egyptian plague word (Ex 9:18-26): 'YHWH rained hail (בָּרָד) upon the land of Egypt.' The Hebrew author completes the Exodus plague cycle: the bowls began with boils (שחין, plague 6) and end with hail (ברד, plague 7), framing the entire sequence as a new Exodus.

Uses מְחָרְפִים (mecharfim — 'reviling/reproaching', from charaf H2778). This is the verb Goliath used against Israel — 1 Sam 17:26,36: 'who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy/reproach (חרף) the armies of the living God?' Greek has ἐβλασφήμησαν ('they blasphemed'). Hebrew 'reproach/defy' and Greek 'blaspheme' carry different nuances: the Hebrew implies taunting or defying God's authority (as a warrior defies an army); the Greek implies sacrilegious speech.
Uses נֶגַע (nega — 'plague', H5061) — again the Levitical/Exodus term, consistent throughout the chapter.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὡς ταλαντιαία ('about a talent in weight') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew does not specify the weight of the hail.
Greek adds ὅτι μεγάλη ἐστὶν ἡ πληγὴ αὐτῆς σφόδρα ('for the plague of it was exceedingly great') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Reviled' for charaf captures the defiance/taunting nuance — not merely 'blasphemed.'
'Plague' for nega — completing the Levitical vocabulary used throughout the chapter.
textual_notes: Exodus 9:18,23-24: 'Behold, about this time tomorrow I will rain very heavy hail (בָּרָד כָּבֵד מְאֹד)... YHWH rained hail upon the land of Egypt.' The seventh bowl hail closes the new-Exodus plague cycle.
Joshua 10:11: 'YHWH threw large stones (אבנים גדלות) from heaven upon them... more died from the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.' Heavenly hail as divine warfare.

chapter_notes.summary:
Revelation 16 in Hebrew is structured as a new Exodus plague cycle, with the bowls systematically deploying Torah plague vocabulary: שחין פרח (boils breaking out — plague 6, Ex 9:9), דם (blood — plague 1, Ex 7:20), חשך (darkness — plague 9, Ex 10:21), צפרדעים (frogs — plague 2, Ex 7:27), ברד (hail — plague 7, Ex 9:18). The Greek text uses generic terms (sore, blood, darkness, spirits, hail) that lack these specific Exodus connections.

The chapter contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers: (1) שחין פרח — the exact Exodus plague phrase (v2), (2) פסל — the Decalogue 'graven image' word (v2), (3) המתפללים — the prayer-verb for idol worship echoing בית התפלה (v2), (4) בארות — 'wells' vs Greek 'rivers and springs' (v4), (5) the ההיה והוה formula playing on the divine name YHWH (v5), (6) Psalm 79:3 verbatim quotation 'poured out blood like water' (v6), (7) שרצים — 'creeping things' vs Greek 'spirits' (v12), (8) תנין — primordial serpent vs Greek 'dragon' (v12), (9) מסלה — Isaiah's prophetic highway (v11), (10) חרון אפו — the specific OT anger compound (v18), (11) הרים וגבעות — the prophetic mountains-and-hills merism vs Greek 'islands and mountains' (v19), (12) תשובה — return-to-God repentance vs Greek mind-change (v9).

Notably, Greek 16:11 is entirely absent from the Hebrew text, which has only 20 verses to the Greek's 21. The Hebrew moves directly from the fifth bowl (darkness, v10) to the sixth bowl (Euphrates, v11). Greek 16:11 repeats the blasphemy-and-non-repentance formula already present in Hebrew v9 — the Hebrew author apparently saw this repetition as unnecessary.

The Hebrew also consistently uses YHWH (יהוה) where Greek has 'God' (Θεός), אלהי הצבאות where Greek has 'God Almighty,' and השטן ('the Adversary') where Greek has 'demons' — maintaining OT divine name theology throughout.
